item.title: Yes, AI Is Being Used for Dating Profile Photos
item.description:
Mating

Yes, AI Is Being Used for Dating Profile Photos

Use your long-term priorities—not just looks—to screen potential matches.

Posted October 25, 2026

Key points
  • An increasing number of dating profile photos seem to have been altered by AI a little—or even a lot.
  • One has to decide how much AI alteration they can tolerate on dating apps and know how to detect such photos.
  • It's best to remain skeptical of dating profile photos and de-prioritize them when judging candidates.
Source: igovar igovar / Pexels

Let's be realistic. What's the first thing you look at when it comes to judging dating profiles? Is it the values and goals listed? Is it whether the person is “fluent in sarcasm," "loves adventure," or emotionally intelligent? Umm, chances are it's actually the photos because, admit it, if you are human, you can be quite superficial—at least in the beginning screening stages. But these days, you've got to wonder how realistic photos on a dating profile even are.

AI May Be Making Dating Profile Photos Even Less Realistic

That's because you may be seeing more photos that have been altered by AI. This can range from AI touch-ups to massive transformations. Yep, surprise, surprise, manipulation can be part of the dating game. It can leave you wondering even more what's real versus not real on a dating app.

I say "even more" because it's not as if things have been totally real all this time. With filters and photoshopping, what you see has long been not necessarily what you'll get. Using AI, though, can significantly step up daters' A-games—meaning, in this case, their alteration games. It can be like hiring a team to help. And that team can transform and even completely generate photos in a matter of seconds, even for those whose own artistic skills consist of not much more than being able to draw a slightly asymmetrical smiley face.

Decide How Much AI You Are Willing to Tolerate

Now, there is the argument that not all AI-alterations of dating profile photos are necessarily bad—as long as there's no intent to deceive. Some may argue that an AI-alteration is like wearing some make-up, changing the lighting, or choosing a different outfit. It helps bring out a person's true self more. Of course, that wouldn't apply if you've used AI to alter your photo to the point that one of your exes looking at the photo were to say, "Who is this? I'd really like to get to know this person."

Others may argue, though, that any use of AI to alter dating photos is not a good look. That it reflects at least some intent to deceive. The argument is that people should be willing to just be their authentic selves.

So what's the right answer? Well, you've got to determine for yourself what you may be fine with versus not fine with, and where you are going to draw the AI line. Remember, dating is about finding the right mutual fit for you.

Look for Evidence of AI Manipulation

Source: Nicolle Kreisch from Pexels

Regardless of where you fall on the OK-versus-not-OK-with-AI spectrum, it will be helpful in general to develop more of an eye for AI—meaning skills at detecting AI-generated images. Know the giveaways, like any distortions or mistakes, such as a person having too many fingers, especially on the periphery of the image where the AI tool and the user may not be checking carefully.

Also, AI-generated images may still have somewhat of an unreal feel to them—like faces looking too polished or even waxy. So, if you feel that something is amiss—or a-mister—you may be right.

This will likely get tougher and tougher, though, as AI technology gets better and better. And users get better and better at working with AI. Plus, guess what else may be helping the AI? Yes, good old-fashioned humans—paid consultants who work with AI and clients to develop dating profile photos for them, meaning dating profiles for the clients and not the AI. So, this is becoming quite an arms race—and a legs, nose, eyes, mouth, butt, and chest race.

See What Dating Apps Are Doing About AI-Generated Photos

As this race escalates, naturally, dating apps may be more apt to do something about it. Otherwise, the risk is that the apps get inundated with AI-generated content, making the apps less attractive to use by humans. Therefore, you may want to check out the AI policies of whatever dating apps you may be considering.

More specifically, see if the apps allow AI-generated dating profile photos. And if not, how exactly do the apps detect such photos? Do they rely on users to report suspicious images, or do they use AI to detect and fight AI? And how good is the AI at detecting AI? And what's done about any suspect photos?

Regardless, don't rely on dating apps solely to keep you safe from being faked. That could be kind of like relying on a grocery store to present only healthy food to you. Dating apps, after all, are businesses, so caveat emptor. It's really up to you—the consumer—to protect yourself.

Be Skeptical of All Dating Profile Photos

One thing that you can do to protect yourself is to maintain a healthy skepticism for all photos on dating apps. Don't assume that someone looks a certain way until you actually see them IRL—meaning "in real life." Treat dating profile pics—and dating profiles in general—as you would those male enhancement advertisements. Beware of any big claims, and only believe things after you've witnessed them in person.

Try to De-emphasize the Dating Profile Photo

Another thing that you can do is de-prioritize looks when searching for possible matches. Yeah, I know, that is easier said than done. For all the talk people have about looking for what's inside a potential partner, it's often the outside—meaning the face and body—that wins at the beginning. You don't see too many people saying, "I can't stop looking at her personality description" or "Oh, look at how big his values are, I really want to talk to him."

Nonetheless, consciously force yourself to use other screening criteria. Decide what is truly important to you in the long run, and then find some way to search for that on the app. Also, try not to rule people in and out based solely on their photos.

Consider Other IRL Dating Avenues

The rise of AI could further fuel the backlash against dating apps and the trend towards wanting more authentic and IRL ways to meet people. I referred to this trend when I covered the whole "meet cute" trend for "A Funny Bone to Pick." Until folks have developed AI that can alter someone's appearance in person, seeing a person live and in the flesh, so to speak, is the best way to figure out what's real and what's not.

item.title: What a Lighthouse Taught Me About Feeling Overwhelmed
item.description:
Mindfulness

What a Lighthouse Taught Me About Feeling Overwhelmed

A familiar painting helped me feel grounded amid the waves of everyday life.

Posted October 25, 2026

Key points
  • Familiar objects can give us a spot to return to when daily responsibilities feel overwhelming all at once.
  • A significant image may help us observe our thoughts without reacting to each one as it comes along.
  • Remembering a personally significant object may help us reconnect with an earlier sense of steadiness.
  • Returning our attention to a familiar object can renew its significance as our circumstances and needs change.

One morning, I woke up with the semester already pressing on me. There were papers to grade and a conference presentation to prepare. Rejected manuscripts needed revisions and new journals to consider. Committee work required more reading and evaluation. New paper ideas, which usually excited me, had joined everything else waiting for my attention.

I was still in my bedroom, and I already felt behind.

Then I looked at a painting on the wall.

A friend had given it to me when I lived in Pennsylvania more than a decade ago. A pale lighthouse stands on a rocky shoreline beside a small building with a red roof. Turquoise waves break against the rocks, sending white spray into the air. The sun sits low on the horizon, spreading yellow and peach across the sky. Light glows through the curve of a wave. Birds glide above the water.

I had always loved its colors. That morning, my attention settled on the lighthouse.

Lighthouse
Source: Sothy Eng

I began imagining everything a lighthouse encounters. Waves rise and fall around it. Weather changes. The sun heats its surface, and night brings cooler air. Through all of this, it remains there.

For a moment, I thought about its strength. Then even the question of strength seemed unnecessary. The lighthouse was simply standing. I could look at it without asking whether I was strong enough to face the day.

I kept looking.

The grading came into my thoughts again. Then a rejected paper. Then something I needed to finish for a committee. Each concern arrived with its own weight. In the painting, I could see waves gathering, curling, and breaking. Gradually, I began recognizing a similar movement in my mind.

Here was the thought about grading. Here came the worry about publication. Another idea followed before the previous one had settled.

As I returned my attention to the lighthouse, I felt more grounded. A few minutes became perhaps half an hour. I watched the painting and noticed my thoughts coming and going.

The work remained. I could begin to see the concerns individually and give myself a little room before responding.

Seeing the waves

Psychologists use the term decentering to describe a way of observing our internal experiences. In a review, Amit Bernstein and colleagues describe processes that include noticing thoughts, experiencing some separation from them, and becoming less reactive to their content. This offers one way to understand what I experienced that morning. I was becoming aware of the movement of my thoughts and how quickly each one demanded my attention.

The painting made this process concrete. “Observe your thoughts” can feel abstract when everything is happening at once. The sea gave my thoughts a visible form. The lighthouse gave my attention somewhere to return.

Later that day, when another concern arrived, I could picture the lighthouse easily. I remembered the water moving around it. That image helped me reconnect with the steadiness I had felt in the bedroom.

I was surprised by how readily it came back to me. A painting I had looked past for years had become available in my mind.

Something to return to

Personally significant images can affect how we experience difficult moments. In a laboratory study, Naomi Eisenberger and colleagues found that women viewing photographs of their romantic partners reported less experimentally induced pain than when viewing control images. The study concerned physical pain and supportive relationships, and it offers evidence that an image can evoke something psychologically consequential through what it represents to us.

My experience with the lighthouse painting strengthened an idea I've held for some time, which I am developing as Enduring Symbolic Theory (EST). I use that name for the possibility that personally significant objects can become recurring points of return, helping us reconnect with a sense of steadiness through seeing and remembering them. (This is a developing proposal drawn from reflection; research would be needed to examine when and how this process works.)

What interests me is the endurance of the symbol. The painting remains on my wall but its image is also available when I am somewhere else. I can return to it across different moments of the day.

A photograph of someone we love might serve a similar purpose. So might a gift associated with someone whose presence reassures us. The significance comes from our relationship with the object and what becomes available when we attend to it.

In an earlier reflection about my aging parents, I wrote about appreciating the physical abilities that make an ordinary morning possible. Making coffee, holding a cup, and sitting quietly can become occasions for gratitude. On other days, contemplating the possibility of simply being has helped me settle.

Different situations may call for different ways of returning to ourselves. That morning, the lighthouse gave form to the overwhelm I was experiencing and offered somewhere to rest my attention.

You might begin with something already in your surroundings. Take a moment to look at it. Notice what it brings to mind and how you feel in its presence. Its significance may become apparent slowly.

If the lighthouse speaks to you, try picturing the weather around it. Small waves could represent everyday tasks asking for your attention. Heat from the sun might resemble pressure building through a demanding day. Strong wind could represent an unexpected disruption, and a storm might resemble several worries arriving together. Let each image reflect how the experience feels to you.

Include the pleasant weather, too. A cool breeze might resemble the ease you feel after a good meal, an afternoon with friends, or a comforting thought. Give these moments your attention. Notice how they feel in your body and allow yourself to enjoy them. They, too, can help you feel grounded.

Throughout the day, gently ask yourself, “What is the weather around my lighthouse right now?” Notice what arrives, how it changes, and what follows. Both the storm and the breeze belong in this practice. You can observe each one without needing to change it immediately.

My painting had been there through many busy mornings. Familiarity had made it easy to overlook, and I imagine I will overlook it again. Yet now, when a wave of worry arrives or a moment of ease invites me to pause, I sometimes remember the lighthouse. I picture the evening light and the water moving around the rocks. I give myself a moment to stand there, too.

Source: OpenAI

item.title: Why There’s No Right Way to Grieve
item.description:
Grief

Why There’s No Right Way to Grieve

Understanding grief can change how we support one another.

Posted October 25, 2026

Key points
  • Grief is a deeply human response to loss rather than a problem to fix, and it looks different for each of us.
  • Expectations about how grief should look or last can leave us feeling as though we are mourning the wrong way.
  • Letting go of expectations about grief can change how we make sense of our losses and support one another.

Most of us have been told, in one way or another, that grief is something to get over. We hear it in well-intended phrases about moving on or finding closure, which suggest that mourning follows a predictable pattern and ends in due time, though grief rarely cooperates with that schedule. Bereavement scholars describe grief, however painful, as a natural, deeply human response to loss rather than a problem to be fixed, and one that looks different for each of us. Understanding why there is no single right way to grieve can change how we make sense of our own losses and how we show up for one another.

Grief Rarely Moves in Stages

Grief is often pictured as a staircase, with denial on the bottom step and acceptance at the top. This notion is largely credited to Elisabeth Kübler-Ross, whose 1969 book, On Death and Dying, outlined five stages observed in terminally ill patients as they came to terms with their own deaths, rather than people mourning a loss. While this work gave us a helpful starting point, the stages have been widely misread as a sequence everyone who grieves "should" move through—a belief experts now caution against. As noted in On Grief and Grieving, Kübler-Ross's final book with coauthor David Kessler, the stages “were never meant to help tuck messy emotions into neat packages.”

In reality, grief comes in waves, returning when we least expect it and, now and then, and offering moments of unexpected beauty along the way. We might keep it all together at the funeral and feel the loss more sharply months later, or find that an anniversary or a favorite song stirs everything up again years down the road. There is no set timeline for mourning, and the kindest response, for ourselves and for others, is to let grief take the time it takes.

Grief Is More Than Sadness

Most of us have learned to read grief by its outward signs, watching for tears at the service or a heaviness in someone’s voice. Yet grief is not one-dimensional, and sadness is seldom the only emotion it brings forward. Often, it is a messy, swirling mix of heartache and hope, confusion and anger, and even moments of stillness. There is a societal assumption that someone is only grieving if they cry or talk openly about their pain, but people cope in very different ways. Some of us stay busy, while others need to tell and retell the story, and research suggests people move between the two, facing the loss at times and taking a break from it at others. No response is more genuine than another, and no manner of response measures how much someone mattered to us.

We Grieve More Losses Than We Realize

We tend to associate grief with death, but it can come with loss of any type. It can arrive with the end of a relationship, a job that once gave our days meaning, a dream we had for ourselves, or a sense of who we are. Scholars sometimes refer to these as living or non-death losses, and although they may not look like mourning from the outside, they can be all-consuming and painful in ways that catch us off guard.

Much of their weight comes from the way one loss can ripple outward into other parts of our lives. Losing a job can also cost us our daily routine and sense of purpose; a breakup can take with it shared friends and a future we had imagined together. Reminders can appear in the most ordinary moments, sometimes long after others expect us to have moved on. In fact, grieving these losses can share many features with mourning a death.

Living losses can be harder to bear when others overlook them entirely. Kenneth Doka (1989) coined the term disenfranchised grief to describe loss that is not openly acknowledged or socially supported. This kind of grief often goes unrecognized by those around us because the loss is not viewed as significant, leaving people unsure whether their grief will be understood or even accepted. Such losses can pass without sympathy cards or casseroles, or a ritual to mark them. Without that recognition, we may be left to mourn on our own, sometimes without knowing that the heaviness we feel is grief. Recognizing these losses as grief, in ourselves and in others, can be the first step toward honoring them. Importantly, there is no typical loss, and so there is no typical way to grieve.

Grief Can Heal Without Closure

Closure is widely considered the goal of grief—a point at which a loss is finally resolved and we can put it behind us. Pauline Boss (2022) argues that closure is largely a myth, and that healing comes from learning to live with the absence rather than resolving it. In other words, moving forward does not require letting go.

Keeping a loss close, through stories or traditions, can be part of grieving well. We might continue telling a friend’s funniest jokes or cook a grandmother’s recipe each holiday, small acts which are a common feature of mourning. Once we stop treating closure as the finish line, no one can say exactly where grief should end, which frees us to offer ourselves and others a little more grace.

Becoming Grief Literate

Understanding grief in these ways is central to grief literacy, an approach to loss recognizing that all of us can learn to be there for people who are grieving, ourselves included. This matters all the more since support from friends and family frequently fades precisely when it may be needed most. The smallest gestures can make a difference, such as replacing the classic “let me know if you need anything” with a specific offer, like picking up groceries or checking in on a difficult anniversary. We can extend that same care to ourselves, whether by acknowledging our own grief or giving it the time it needs.

There is no right way to grieve. There is, however, room for more kindness toward ourselves and one another.

item.title: Acknowledging the Mothers Who Did It Tired
item.description:
Resilience

Acknowledging the Mothers Who Did It Tired

Childhood trauma and the resilience of mothers.

Posted October 25, 2026

Source: OLEKSANDR MALIEV/Shutterstock

I rarely scroll through reels online, but when I do, I can easily become consumed. The algorithm, like magic, serves reels with similar content and themes and I can get lost in a time warp.

Recently, one reel caught my attention. It featured a soulful song expressing deep pain and resilience. The lyrics echo what my clients have shared with me for over three decades: mothers—mostly single mothers—who survived child abuse and are now mothering their own children, striving to give them what they did not get as children while fiercely attempting to protect them from the trauma they once endured.

Single motherhood is often synonymous with financial insecurity. Researcher Norman Garmezy found that among all the potential risk factors that mothers with abuse histories encounter, economic burden poses the severest risk because it impacts so many other facets of her life. Particularly, poverty impacts her ability to secure basic needs of food, clothing, and shelter.

In Maslow’s hierarchy of needs, food, clothing, and shelter are the foundations of the pyramid. These must be stable before an individual can accomplish the higher-level needs of safety, security, love and belonging, self-esteem, and, ultimately, the achievement of self-actualization. If a mother struggles with food insecurity or inadequate housing or clothing, it makes it difficult to experience safety, belonging, and self-esteem. The higher-level needs are resources that can only grow in conditions of safety and acceptance.

To escape abuse, many survivors may leave home early and not finish high school, putting them at risk of unemployment or low-wage jobs. If they have children, they frequently end up struggling financially.

Poverty and a history of child abuse increase the stress of parenting, particularly for mothers who carry the economic burdens and responsibilities of raising children alone. My clients expressed feeling stressed and overwhelmed by limited resources. Financial difficulties caused anxiety and forced them to choose between paying utility bills and rent. Mothers also expressed feelings of inadequacy and regret that their economic situation made it difficult to provide a better life for their children.

One client, Lara, was a single mother of a six-year-old boy. She worked full-time as a nurse’s aide and part-time cleaning houses on weekends. She still could not make ends meet. The inflated cost of rent, groceries, and car payments created extra pressure. Despite this, Lara was determined to provide her son with a good education, a safe neighborhood, and positive and caring people in his life.

In one session, on a cold and snowy night, Lara said she was concerned about driving home on slippery roads. The brake pads in her car had worn down and she did not have money in her budget to replace them. As a result, she was braking on the rotors, which made a loud screeching sound when she tried to come to a stop. She was terrified that she would run a red light and cause a crash.

In a session, another client, Elaine, recounted an experience she had when getting her re-certification for food stamps. While taking her photo ID, instead of telling her to "smile" before taking the picture, the worker told her to "smile and say sex”. Elaine complied. As she told me what happened she started to cry. She could not articulate what the tears were about, or the feelings of despair associated with them. However, as we processed the event, the parallel became clear: what occurred in the food-stamp office mirrored her childhood abuse experiences. Once again, she was being treated as an object by those in power, was the brunt of a joke for another's entertainment, and was forced to smile and do what she was told to survive.

Throughout my career, I have researched, written on, and lectured about the connection between adverse childhood experiences, poverty, and trauma. In my clinical practice, I saw the palpable impact on mothers who went back to school to lift themselves out of poverty. I watched them balance two jobs, work overtime, raise children, provide their children with food and shelter, and make impossible financial tradeoffs—all the while carrying the lasting consequences of childhood abuse and neglect.

They did it tired. They mothered, pursued higher education, and sacrificed to give their children more than they had growing up, while trying to protect their children from the harmful childhood experiences they suffered. The song "I Did It Tired," while generated by AI, still captures their lived reality and echoes my own memories of being a witness to their pain and struggles as they journeyed from survival to resilience and triumph.

They did it tired, they did it sacred, they did it broke. They fed the mouths, dried the tears, and held their breaths for years and years. They obeyed the voice inside that said don’t quit. They gave too much and gave some more. They bent so far, they almost broke. They swallowed words they should have spoke.

These words speak to their dual journeys as survivors and mothers. Therapy and survivor groups offered these women a safe place to be tired, to cry, to breathe, and to voice their pain. It gave them space to be held with compassion by someone who saw their resilience and courage. It offered a place where they could be seen, heard, and applauded for their strength and honored for their extraordinary perseverance and resilience.
